Training-dataset conventions — COCO / YOLO / VOC and pitfalls in visual inspection

fullseye can emit pixel-perfect ground truth with inspection_dataset / optscene_instances / optscene_defect_mask. But ground truth becomes usable only once it is converted into a form the training framework can read. This document is not a description of ops; it is teaching material on the receiving side — coordinate conventions, the definition of area, the quirks of evaluation metrics, how to build splits. It sits in the same position as optics/guides/mv_*.md (2-D imaging chain) and 3d/guides/depth_sensors.md (3-D imaging chain); this one is the exit.

1. There are 3 bbox representations, and fullseye's is yet another

Accidents happen here 8 times out of ten. The same rectangle can be written as numbers in 4 ways.

| Format | Order | Origin | Unit |

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| COCO | [x, y, width, height] | Top-left, 0-based | Absolute px |

| YOLO (Ultralytics) | class x_center y_center width height | Top-left, 0-based | Normalised by image width and height (0–1) |

| Pascal VOC (XML) | xmin ymin xmax ymax | Top-left | Absolute px, customarily treated as 1-based (inherited from MATLAB). Conversion code is split on whether to apply −1 or not, so do not trust other people's scripts |

| fullseye optscene_instances | (x0, y0, x1, y1) | Top-left, 0-based | Absolute px, bottom-right included (inclusive) |

The bbox of optscene_instances includes the bottom-right, so the width is not x1 − x0 but x1 − x0 + 1. Conversion formulas:

w = x1 - x0 + 1
h = y1 - y0 + 1
coco = [x0, y0, w, h]                                   # absolute px
yolo = [(x0 + w / 2) / W, (y0 + h / 2) / H, w / W, h / H]   # 0-1 normalised

A mix-up of 1 pixel is more fatal the smaller the defect (§4).

2. What is inside COCO (points to pin down from primary sources)

• bbox is (x, y, width, height) in absolute coordinates — this corresponds to detectron2's BoxMode.XYWH_ABS (whereas XYXY_ABS is (x1,y1,x2,y2)).

• segmentation takes 3 forms, and pycocotools distinguishes and handles them:

1. Polygon (list) — [x1, y1, ..., xn, yn] per connected component

2. Uncompressed RLE (a dict whose counts is a list)

3. Compressed RLE ({"size": [h, w], "counts": ...}, LEB128 variable length)

• RLE masks are column-major. The specification of pycocotools.mask decides it so. numpy defaults to row-major, so forgetting np.asarray(mask, order="F") makes the mask collapse into a meaningless shape that is neither a transpose nor a flip. This breaks silently, so it is hard to notice.

• RLE is "a sequence of run lengths", and the odd-numbered entries are always runs of 0 (e.g. M=[0 0 1 1 1 0 1] → counts=[2 3 1 1]). For a mask that begins with 1, counts starts from 0.

• area is the area of the mask (or polygon), not the area of the bbox. For a long thin scratch it is a fraction of the bbox area. The small/medium/large classification in §3 uses this area, so filling it with the bbox area makes the evaluation a different thing.

• iscrowd=1 means "1 thing as a crowd" and receives special treatment at evaluation: it is not penalised whether it is hit or missed. If you do not understand it, do not set it (detectron2's advice says the same).

• category_id is [0, num_categories-1] (detectron2's convention). The official COCO data itself is 1-based with gaps, so using raw COCO as indices directly shifts everything by 1.

3. What is inside the evaluation metrics (do not take mAP at face value)

Defaults of pycocotools (cocoeval.Params):

| Parameter | Value |

| --- | --- |

| IoU thresholds | 0.50, 0.55, ..., 0.95 (10 steps) |

| Recall thresholds | 0.00 … 1.00 (101 steps) |

| Area ranges | all = [0, 1e10] / small = area < 32² = 1024 px² / medium = 32²–96² / large > 96² |

| maxDets | 1, 10, 100 |

Where this bites in visual inspection:

• The small threshold of 1024 px² is an absolute value. Everything under 32×32 px falls into small. Nearly all tiny defects in inspection go here, so if you report, AP_small is the number that means anything.

• maxDets=100 — if 1 image has more than 100 defects (powdery foreign matter, clusters of dents), that alone caps recall. For applications that count particles, the default cannot measure it.

• IoU 0.5 is too strict for small objects. For the same absolute error, the smaller the box, the more the IoU collapses:

| Box size | 1 px off | 2 px | 3 px | 4 px |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| 10 × 10 px | 0.82 | 0.67 | 0.54 | 0.43 (fail) |

| 100 × 100 px | 0.98 | 0.96 | 0.94 | 0.92 |

A 10 px defect is counted as a "missed detection" when it is just 4 px off. A position-accuracy problem

turns into a detection-rate problem, so for tiny defects it matches reality better to lower the IoU threshold, or to measure by centre distance or

pixel IoU (segm). Do not conclude "the detection rate is low" without changing the metric.

4. Pitfalls specific to visual inspection

1. Good parts have no annotations. COCO allows "images with 0 annotations", and YOLO states explicitly that "images without objects need no .txt". Yet many training scripts silently discard images with empty annotations. If they are discarded, not even 1 good image enters training, and you get a model that "always outputs some defect". First, count whether the number of good images matches the number in the training log.

2. Extreme class imbalance. Defect pixels are on the order of 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁶ of all pixels. A result where pixel-level accuracy is 99.99% but the content is empty comes out all the time. 1 number does not distinguish "perfect" from "outputs nothing", so always report recall on defect pixels and the number of false detections separately.

3. Leakage across the split. In synthetic data, several images from the same base material and the same random-number lineage easily end up on both the train and val sides. Even if domain randomisation makes them look different, the same defect layout is effectively the same sample. Form groups from the seed of inspection_dataset and the defect labels, and split by group (not by image).

4. Synthetic data has labels that are too perfect. Annotations on real data are drawn by people, so boundaries wobble by a few px and tiny defects get overlooked. A model trained only on perfect ground truth, when evaluated on real data, has the wobble on the annotation side counted against it as false detections. The sim2real gap is not only in the appearance of the images but also in the quality of the labels.

5. Do not throw away meta. inspection_dataset returns lighting type, exposure, amount of perturbation and defect labels in meta. This is not needed for training, but it is needed for isolating failures ("it fails only under dark field" cannot be seen without meta).

5. Exporting from fullseye (correspondence table)

| What you want | Where it comes from in fullseye | Conversion |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Image | inspection_dataset(...)["image"] | As is (already quantised) |

| bbox | optscene_instances(...)["bbox"] (inclusive) | To COCO / YOLO with the formulas in §1 |

| Class | Same, ["kind"] | Map to category_id. Align to 0-based |

| Instance mask | Same, ["mask"] (H×W bool) | RLE-encode column-major (§2) |

| Area | Same, ["area_px"] | Put into COCO's area (not the bbox area) |

| Semantic mask | optscene_defect_mask | For segmentation training |

| Depth ground truth | inspection_dataset(...)["depth_mm"] | Unit mm. Carry the scale along |

| Reproduction info | Same, ["meta"] | Keep in the dataset's info / custom fields |

6. Current gaps (honestly)

• There is no export op. All the conversions above are currently hand-written. Not even 1 op emits COCO JSON / YOLO txt (or reads them in the reverse direction).

• There is no group-split op. There is no means of preventing the leakage in §4-3 mechanically.

• There is no means of imitating label wobble. As in §4-4, ground truth being too perfect is a domain gap in itself, but there is no op that deliberately blurs boundaries.

7. Diagnostic table — from symptom to cause

| Symptom | Suspect first | How to check |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Signs that not a single good image was learned | Images with empty annotations are being dropped by the loader | Compare the image count in the training log with the generated count |

| Pixel accuracy 99.99% yet nothing is output | Class imbalance | Report recall on defect pixels and the number of false detections separately |

| val results are too good | Leakage across the split (the same seed and same defect layout on both sides) | Form groups from seed and defect labels, re-split by group and retrain |

| AP is low only for small defects | IoU 0.5 is strict on small boxes (table in §3) | Re-measure by centre distance or pixel IoU (segm) |

| All boxes are off by 1 px / everything fails | Inclusive vs exclusive mix-up, VOC's 1-based origin | Draw the converted bboxes on the image and check by eye (do not look only at numbers) |

| Masks collapse into meaningless shapes | RLE was built row-major | Rebuild with order="F" (§2) |

| Recall plateaus when 1 image has many defects | maxDets=100 | Raise maxDets and re-evaluate |

| Good on synthetic data but full of false detections on real data | Difference in label quality (ground truth too perfect) | Redraw the GT for a few real images, measure the boundary wobble and reflect it on the synthetic side |

| Class numbers are off by 1 | category_id in raw COCO data is 1-based with gaps | Output the category list and explicitly build a dictionary mapping it to consecutive numbers |
